summary:
Rājasthān stands under India's national framework on gender identity, and no state-level deviation from that framework has been sourced. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026 was passed by both houses of India's Parliament in March 2026 and awaits presidential assent, so the recognition rules a visitor encounters in this state are those of the amended national statute.

The amendment removes the right to self-identification that the 2014 Supreme Court third-gender judgment had established and that the 2019 Act carried forward. Legal recognition is now limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people fall outside the recognition scheme entirely, and recognition is tied to medical certification rather than to the applicant's own declaration.

Human Rights Watch described the bill as a major setback on 26 March 2026, stating that it strips thousands of people of rights and increases their exposure to risk. As national law it sets the recognition baseline for visitors and residents in every Indian state and union territory, Rājasthān included.

Opposition parties and LGBTQ organisations protested the bill's passage. The government argues that the change widens access to welfare benefits, while critics hold that it excludes transgender, non-binary and gender-fluid people from legal recognition altogether.

Recognition remains uneven in practice, and the discrimination the amended regime sits alongside continues in education, healthcare and formal employment across the country. A trans visitor to Rājasthān should therefore expect document encounters governed by medical certification, and should not assume that a self-declared gender marker will be accepted by state authorities.
tangentialFactors:
India's wider baseline is mixed rather than uniformly hostile. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex has been interpreted to cover gender identity and sexual orientation, with the Allahabad High Court extending this to employment in 2021. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened with the 2024 replacement of the Indian Penal Code by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which dropped the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that had protected trans persons; trans communities report fearing a rise in assaults as a result.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a recurring source of friction. In November 2024 the openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain was stopped at Chennai International Airport by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card; in February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person asked to undergo a medical examination by passport authorities; and a transwoman in Kolkata alleged groping by a Railway Protection Force constable under the pretext of a gender check, while trans people held by railway police in Assam have described degrading custody treatment.

Assessments of police conduct diverge on the record. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, whereas victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.

The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued broad guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities; conversion therapy nonetheless continues through clandestine networks despite that judgment and the National Medical Commission's 2022 ban.
localsOnly:
Residents of Rājasthān draw welfare and recognition from the national scheme, since the state has not been sourced as running its own transgender welfare board. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha operate such boards, coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits to hijras; those arrangements are not documented here.

The Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

For a resident seeking legal recognition under the amended statute, medical certification is now the gateway, and self-identification outside the hijra, kinner or intersex categories does not establish a claim. Employment, education and healthcare discrimination remain documented features of daily life.

Intersex residents face a documented pattern of non-consensual assignment surgeries in infancy, including a parental preference for assigning male; the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants, but reports record a longer history of infanticide and unregulated operations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill had not received presidential assent as of the March 2026 reporting, so the operative text and its commencement date remain unresolved in these sources.

No source in this inventory reports how Rājasthān police, passport offices or state hospitals apply the amended recognition rules in practice; enforcement in this state is therefore unresolved rather than assessed.

The distribution of hate-crime protection for gender-motivated violence after the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita took effect in 2024 is not established here, and the divergence between the UK policy note and the June 2024 victim interviews on police abuse is left unresolved.

Rājasthān-specific data on facilities, shelters, healthcare provision and partner recognition were not sourced for this record.
